paras: We write to express our concern over recent developments in Hong Kong and to urge your Department to determine whether Hong Kong Police Commissioner Joe Chow Yat-ming (周一鳴 ) meets the criteria for sanctions pursuant to the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, the Hong Kong Autonomy Act, and Executive Order 13936.

During your confirmation hearing before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, you testified on the critical importance of “a commitment to democracy and human rights.” In March of this year, as Secretary of State, you acted on these principles by sanctioning six Beijing and Hong Kong officials for their recent role in undermining Hong Kong’s autonomy.1 Unfortunately, Chinese Communist Party-directed officials in Hong Kong continue to undermine its autonomy and freedoms. Most notably, on June 6, local authorities levied new charges against pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong under the city’s National Security Law, alleging conspiracy to collude with a foreign country.2 These developments paint a disturbing picture that the CCP seeks to keep Wong, who is currently serving a nearly five-year sentence, behind bars for life. The CCP is targeting other like-minded individuals as well, and its repression in Hong Kong is not limited to the most prominent activists. On the anniversary of the CCP’s Tiananmen Square Massacre, police flooded the streets, intimidating mourners and passerbys alike. Numerous

1 Office of the Spokesperson, U.S. Sanctions Six Individuals for Undermining Hong Kong’s Autonomy, U.S. Department of State, March 31, 2025, https://www.state.gov/u-s-sanctions-six-individuals-for-undermining-hongkongs-autonomy/

2 Jessia Pang and James Pomfret, “Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong faces second charge under national security law,” Reuters, June 6, 2025, https://www.reuters.com/world/china/hong-kong-activist-joshua-wong-faces-second-charge-under-national-security-law-2025-06-06/

individuals were detained for simple gestures such as holding flowers, displaying electric candles, and gathering in a local park.3 Your March 2025 decision to levy sanctions on then-Hong Kong Police Commissioner Raymond Siu sent a message that the United States stands with Hong Kongers. However, just days after the sanctions were announced, Siu retired, ushering in a new official to abide by Beijing’s orders. For this reason, we urge the Department of State to review these developments and determine whether Commissioner Chow meets the criteria for sanctions pursuant to the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, the Hong Kong Autonomy Act, and Executive Order 13936. Thank you for your attention to human rights and the oppression of the CCP. Our committee is closely monitoring the CCP’s efforts to dismantle human rights around the world, and we look forward to your timely action on these important issues.

3 James Lee, “2 arrested, 10 taken away by Hong Kong police on Tiananmen crackdown anniversary, Hong Kong Free Press, June 5, 2025, https://hongkongfp.com/2025/06/05/2-arrested-10-taken-away-by-hong-kong-police-on-tiananmen-crackdown-anniversary/
